Delegating Authorization to Misaligned Agents:
Coalitional Alignment and Safe Control

Natalie Collina    Surbhi Goel    Aaron Roth    Sikata Sengupta
Abstract

Long-running AI agents create a control problem: each action they take changes the state, which in turn affects the trajectory of future actions. If the agent is not fully aligned, then guaranteeing safety requires approving consequential actions before allowing them to be executed. But requiring human approval at every step makes attention a bottleneck. Delegating review to other AI agents raises the same alignment problem: the reviewers may themselves be misaligned. We identify a condition on a reviewing panel that is weaker than individual alignment yet necessary and sufficient for a guarantee that the principal fares at least as well in expectation as under a designated baseline policy.

Each reviewer agent reports whether an action proposal made by a proposer agent improves its own utility relative to the baseline. We show that a threshold rule tolerating kk disapprovals is safe exactly when, after any kk reviewers are removed, the principal’s utility can be written as a nonnegative combination of the remaining reviewers’ utilities, plus a term that is nonnegative on every feasible proposal. We call this property kk-robust coalitional alignment. No individual reviewer need be aligned: the condition can arise naturally e.g. when reviewers’ objectives are unbiased but noisy perturbations of the principal’s. The characterization lifts to sequential control: in a discounted Markov decision process with an arbitrary history-dependent proposer agent, local safety at every state is both necessary and sufficient for the induced policy to match or improve the baseline in expected discounted utility.

When reviewers vote strategically, full-panel coverage in reward-function space guarantees that every Nash equilibrium is safe under the unanimous approval rule; in contrast, more permissive thresholds can admit unsafe equilibria even when reviewers are individually aligned. Finally, we establish an information-theoretic limit of binary approval: when feasible lotteries include both gains and losses for the principal, exact safety and completeness require an aligned reviewer.

This impossibility can be circumvented either by allowing approximation error or by eliciting richer information from reviewers. Experiments with existing reviewer models show that collective review can remain sound without an aligned individual, even when some disapprovals are tolerated. Using numerical scores allows more beneficial proposals to be authorized at comparable soundness.

1 Introduction

As AI systems become more capable, users are increasingly using them to act on their behalf in long-running tasks: allowing them e.g. to write and execute code, send messages, and initiate transactions. A conservative safety policy would require a person to authorize every consequential action—but this makes human attention a bottleneck that negates most of the advantages of task automation. Modern systems have therefore begun to delegate part of this authorization process. For example, Codex’s Auto-review mode sends a proposed action to an approval subagent, which is empowered to authorize actions on the user’s behalf without interrupting the user (OpenAI, 2026).

But delegating approval to other AI agents creates an apparent circularity. The principal’s main AI system—the proposer agent—was placed behind an approval boundary for fear that it may be misaligned and so may not faithfully pursue the user’s interests. Requiring the reviewer to be perfectly aligned is a poor solution to this problem, since the problem is predicated on perfect alignment being a difficult goal. We ask whether a weaker alignment condition can still guarantee that the principal is at least as well off as under a baseline policy. We show that it can.

1.1 Model and safety guarantee

In our model the principal begins by designating a baseline policy, such as refusing tool calls or following some weaker but known-to-be-safe controller. At each state, the proposer agent proposes an alternative to the baseline action. This proposal (a possibly randomized action) is sent to a panel of external reviewers. Each reviewer compares the proposal with the baseline according to its own objective and returns an approval or disapproval vote represented as a single bit. An aggregation rule sees the set of reviewers who approve and decides whether to execute the proposal; if the proposal is rejected, the system follows the action induced by the baseline policy. We allow any deterministic rule based on this approval set; threshold rules are the canonical example.

We call an authorization rule sound if it provides a safety guarantee relative to the baseline policy. In a one-decision model, this means that every executed proposal weakly increases the principal’s expected utility over a designated baseline action. In a sequential MDP model, it means that the policy induced by repeated authorization has expected discounted principal utility at least that of consistently following the baseline policy. The guarantee holds for every feasible proposal, initial state, and history-adaptive proposer agent, and applies in expectation over the randomness of the proposed action distributions and underlying state transition probabilities.

1.2 Our results

Our core results are exact characterizations of safe threshold review and safe sequential control. We extend these results to fully strategic reviewers and the equilibria their behavior induces, under a stronger coverage condition on their reward functions. Finally we establish an information-theoretic impossibility on the kind of binary-vote approval mechanism we study, and briefly consider two routes around it. We state the main results informally here, with pointers to their precise versions.

Static safety.

We begin by isolating a single authorization decision under a threshold rule that executes a proposal when it receives at most kk disapproval votes.

We say that a subpanel covers the principal if the principal’s utility is a nonnegative combination of the subpanel’s utilities, plus a term that is nonnegative on every feasible proposal. The panel is kk-robustly coalitionally aligned if this coverage condition survives the deletion of any kk reviewers.

Informal result (Coalitional alignment characterizes threshold safety).

The kk-tolerant threshold rule is sound if and only if the panel is kk-robustly coalitionally aligned.

Theorem 1 and Corollary 2 give the precise statements. Coverage by the full panel (the case k=0k=0) characterizes whether any sound rule that accepts unanimous approval exists, and the same coalitional condition extends to arbitrary monotone rules through the coalitions whose approval is just sufficient to authorize a proposal. The same characterization also identifies the most permissive sound monotone rule (which is not necessarily a threshold rule): Authorize an action exactly when it is unanimously approved by some approval set that covers the principal (Proposition 1). Coalitional alignment can hold even when every reviewer is individually misaligned, so it is strictly weaker than full alignment. Certifying that a particular panel satisfies it may still be difficult, but implementing a threshold rule requires only counting binary votes, and our theorems characterize exactly when doing so is safe.

Sequential control.

The one-decision model is a warm-up for authorization in a discounted Markov decision process. In this model, at state ss, reviewer ii votes on the counterfactual “take the proposed action once, then follow the baseline policy,” evaluated with its own baseline-policy QQ-function, and compares it with the alternative of running the baseline policy forever. The deployed system need not actually return to the baseline after one step: the proposer agent observes the new state and may submit another proposal that depends on the entire history. Reviewers therefore need not—and at the time of voting cannot—evaluate the full trajectory that ultimately unfolds. Nevertheless, the principal’s expected gain over the baseline equals the expected discounted sum of these one-step gains along the actual trajectory, which yields our main control result.

Informal result (Local safety is equivalent to global safety).

Repeated authorization is safe against every history-adaptive proposer agent if and only if every proposal that can be authorized has nonnegative principal baseline advantage at the state where it is proposed. For threshold voting, this holds exactly when robust coalitional alignment holds at every state.

Theorem 2 formalizes this equivalence for arbitrary state-dependent authorization rules and gives the corresponding coalitional characterization for general monotone rules.

Strategic reviewers.

In a one-shot authorization problem, sincere voting is a (weakly) dominant strategy for the reviewers (Proposition 2). But it is no longer dominant in a multi-round problem. We therefore study strategic reviewers directly, allowing them to choose history-dependent voting policies that maximize their own returns along the actual trajectory.

Informal result (Strategic safety under threshold voting).

Under the approval rule that requires reviewer unanimity, full-panel coverage in reward-function space guarantees that every Nash equilibrium is safe. A threshold that tolerates even one disapproval can have unsafe Nash equilibria—even when every reviewer is perfectly aligned. But if every subpanel left after deleting kk reviewers covers the principal’s reward function, safety holds at any equilibrium stable against joint deviations by k+1k+1 reviewers.

Theorem 3 gives the formal guarantee, and Proposition 3 shows why ordinary Nash equilibrium is insufficient for permissive thresholds.

Completeness and the limits of binary approval.

Soundness is a one-sided guarantee that promises safety but not usefulness — a sound approval policy could reject many beneficial proposals. We also study completeness, which requires sufficiently beneficial proposals to be executed. We establish a basic limit on what any binary approval rule can accomplish.

Informal result (A limit of binary approval and two ways around it).

When feasible lotteries include both principal gains and losses, any rule based only on binary votes that always authorizes every principal-acceptable lottery and rejects every harmful one requires an aligned reviewer.

But this requirement does not persist under two relaxations. First we can allow approximate soundness and completeness. Under a simple generative model in which reviewers are noisy perturbations of the principal, majority voting converges to soundness and completeness with high probability even though no reviewer converges to alignment; second, if we allow reviewers to report cardinal utilities rather than binary judgments, we can have both perfect soundness and completeness without an aligned reviewer.

Theorem 4 gives the exact impossibility, Proposition 4 gives the random and deterministic approximation results, and Corollary 9 gives the cardinal-score result.

Supporting appendices record two further results. Appendix D combines arbitrary reports, approximate coverage, and bounded evaluation error into a single robustness guarantee. Appendix E shows that auditing robust coverage is tractable in fixed dimension or at a fixed robustness level, but is coNP-complete even under approximation (Proposition 8).

Experiments.

We study panels of existing reward models and safety evaluators (Section 7). In answer selection, we find that unanimous review can block every lottery over the candidate answers that lowers the probability of a correct answer relative to the baseline, even when each reviewer would approve some such lottery. This gives empirical examples of coalitional alignment without individual alignment. Coverage can also survive reviewer removals, allowing sound review to tolerate disapprovals. Using numerical scores instead of binary votes improves the resulting tradeoff: more correct answers are authorized at comparable soundness. For safety evaluators, the benefit comes from overlapping objections: every harmful response in the evaluation receives multiple disapprovals. Tolerating one disapproval releases more acceptable responses while still withholding every harmful response.

1.3 Related Work

AI Alignment.

The most closely related prior works are Collina et al. (2026a); Collina et al. (2026b), who study “emergent alignment” that results from differently misaligned model providers competing to deploy LLMs that will influence user actions. Like us, these papers ask when an outcome comparable to what could be obtained from perfect alignment can instead be obtained from a weaker population level condition. Our kk-robust coalitional alignment condition is a generalization of their “market alignment” condition (equivalent for k=0k=0) — but the problem we study is very different. In their model users are the only ones who can take action, and the AI providers must compete for user attention in order to influence action. In contrast we study AI agents who are able to act on their own, and study oversight by other AI models who can collectively block action, but are not competing for users in a market.

AI-control protocols and guard agents also delegate oversight to models (Greenblatt et al., 2024; Xiang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025), but the focus of this literature is on detecting intentional subversion or enforcing a specified safety policy. Complementary empirical work shows that partitioning a common set of evaluation criteria across model calls can improve model-based oversight and reduce vulnerability to adversarial presentation (Akinwande et al., 2026).

Economic Theory.

Coalitional alignment is a geometric analogue of aggregating expected-utility preferences under a Pareto condition (Harsanyi, 1955). The winning coalitions and groups that can block authorization in our characterizations are also studied in the theory of simple games (Freixas et al., 2011). Classical expert-panel models aggregate noisy judgments from experts who share a common objective (Nitzan and Paroush, 1983); our reviewers may have genuinely different objectives.

Reinforcement Learning.

Our sequential model is closest to runtime assurance and intervention-based safe RL. The Simplex architecture switches from an advanced controller to a verified baseline controller (Seto et al., 1998); shields and advantage-based intervention similarly filter actions using a trusted specification or safety objective (Alshiekh et al., 2018; Wagener et al., 2021). Safe policy improvement guarantees performance relative to a baseline (Pirotta et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2015; Laroche et al., 2019), and safe RL with binary feedback learns from an oracle that labels actions safe or unsafe (Bennett et al., 2023). We instead aggregate comparisons from reviewers with different rewards and obtain a guarantee against any history-adaptive proposer agent.

2 The one-decision model and geometric preliminaries

We first isolate a single authorization decision. The proposer agent submits an action distribution, and each reviewer compares its induced outcomes with the baseline according to its own utility. We ask when the resulting approvals are sufficient to rule out a loss for the principal, even though the reviewers may have different objectives. Here the feasible outcomes and utility functions are fixed; in Section 4, the same decision problem will recur at each state, with utilities given by continuation values.

2.1 The decision problem and feasible deviations

For any finite set XX, write

Δ⁡(X):={p∈ℝ+X:∑x∈Xpx=1}\Delta(X):=\left\{p\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{X}:\sum_{x\in X}p_{x}=1\right\}

for the simplex of probability distributions on XX.

Definition 2.1 (One-decision authorization problem).

Let Ω\Omega be a finite outcome space. The principal PP and reviewers i∈N:={1,…,n}i\in N:=\{1,\ldots,n\} have arbitrary real-valued utility functions

uj:Ω→ℝ,j∈{P,1,…,n}.u_{j}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R},\qquad j\in\{P,1,\ldots,n\}.

Each participant evaluates a lottery μ∈Δ⁡(Ω)\mu\in\Delta(\Omega) by its expected utility

Uj​(μ):=𝔼ω∼μ​[uj​(ω)]=∑ω∈Ωμ⁡(ω)​uj​(ω).U_{j}(\mu):=\mathbb{E}_{\omega\sim\mu}[u_{j}(\omega)]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\mu(\omega)u_{j}(\omega).

Let A={a0,a1,…,am}A=\{a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}\} be a finite action set. The distinguished action a0a_{0} is the baseline, and each action aa induces an outcome lottery μa∈Δ⁡(Ω)\mu_{a}\in\Delta(\Omega). A proposal is a randomized action q∈Δ⁡(A)q\in\Delta(A), which induces the outcome lottery

μ⁡(q):=∑a∈Aq⁡(a)​μa.\mu(q):=\sum_{a\in A}q(a)\mu_{a}.

Writing μ0:=μa0\mu_{0}:=\mu_{a_{0}}, participant jj’s gain from qq relative to the baseline is

gj​(q):=Uj​(μ⁡(q))−Uj​(μ0).g_{j}(q):=U_{j}(\mu(q))-U_{j}(\mu_{0}).

The utility functions need not bear any particular relationship to one another.

This standard expected-utility model has a convenient geometric representation. Identify each utility function with its vector of values in ℝΩ\mathbb{R}^{\Omega} and each lottery with its probability vector.

Definition 2.2 (Feasible deviations).

The deviation induced by a proposal qq is

d⁡(q):=μ⁡(q)−μ0.d(q):=\mu(q)-\mu_{0}.

For each nonbaseline action, write da:=μa−μ0d_{a}:=\mu_{a}-\mu_{0}. The set of feasible deviations and its conic hull are

𝒟\displaystyle\mathcal{D} :=conv({0}∪{da:a≠a0})={∑a≠a0θada:θa≥0,∑a≠a0θa≤1},\displaystyle:=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{d_{a}:a\neq a_{0}\}\bigr)=\left\{\sum_{a\neq a_{0}}\theta_{a}d_{a}:\theta_{a}\geq 0,\ \sum_{a\neq a_{0}}\theta_{a}\leq 1\right\},
𝒞\displaystyle\mathcal{C} :=cone⁡(𝒟)={∑a≠a0θa​da:θa≥0}.\displaystyle:=\operatorname{cone}(\mathcal{D})=\left\{\sum_{a\neq a_{0}}\theta_{a}d_{a}:\theta_{a}\geq 0\right\}.

Let L:=span⁡(𝒞)L:=\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{C}) be the feasible span. Because deviations are differences between distributions, LL is contained in the zero-sum subspace

H0:={d∈ℝΩ:⟨𝟏,d⟩=0}.H_{0}:=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}:\left\langle\mathbf{1},d\right\rangle=0\}.

Expected-utility gain has the geometric representation

gj​(q)=⟨uj,d⁡(q)⟩,j∈{P,1,…,n}.g_{j}(q)=\left\langle u_{j},d(q)\right\rangle,\qquad j\in\{P,1,\ldots,n\}.

Thus the geometry below is simply a representation of the underlying decision problem.

Multiplying a deviation by a positive constant changes the size of every gain but preserves its sign. Every direction in 𝒞\mathcal{C} can be scaled into 𝒟\mathcal{D}, so exact soundness can be studied on the cone. Bounds on the size of a loss must instead retain the bounded set 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

Intuitively, a reviewer is aligned with the principal if they share the same utility function. The formal definition allows positive rescaling, which does not change binary comparisons, and only compares utilities on feasible deviations.

Definition 2.3 (Individual alignment).

Reviewer ii is aligned with the principal on the feasible span if there is a constant c>0c>0 such that

⟨ui,d⟩=c⁡⟨uP,d⟩for every ​d∈L.\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle=c\,\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\qquad\text{for every }d\in L.

An aligned reviewer and the principal therefore evaluate every feasible direction proportionally; their utility vectors may differ arbitrarily on L⟂L^{\perp}.

2.2 Authorization rules

We assume for now that the reviewers are sincere: reviewer ii approves a proposal with deviation dd when ⟨ui,d⟩≥0\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle\geq 0 and disapproves when ⟨ui,d⟩<0\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle<0. Later we model strategic and noisy reviewers.

Definition 2.4 (Authorization rule).

For a deviation dd, its approval set is the set of reviewers that approve it:

S⁡(d):={i∈N:⟨ui,d⟩≥0}.S(d):=\{i\in N:\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle\geq 0\}.

An authorization rule is a family 𝒲⊆2N\mathcal{W}\subseteq 2^{N} of winning approval sets. A proposal with deviation dd is executed exactly when S⁡(d)∈𝒲S(d)\in\mathcal{W}; otherwise the baseline action is executed. We require N∈𝒲N\in\mathcal{W}—the admissibility condition—so unanimous approval is always sufficient for execution. A rule is monotone if

S∈𝒲​ and ​S⊆T⟹T∈𝒲.S\in\mathcal{W}\text{ and }S\subseteq T\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\in\mathcal{W}.

Requiring N∈𝒲N\in\mathcal{W} excludes the reject-all rule, which is trivially sound but never delegates authorization. Monotonicity says that an additional approval cannot turn execution into rejection.

Definition 2.5 (Minimal winning coalitions).

Let ℳ⁡(𝒲)\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}) be the set of inclusion-minimal winning approval sets.

Every winning set contains a member of ℳ⁡(𝒲)\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}). For a monotone rule, the converse also holds, so

S(d)∈𝒲⟺S⁡(d) contains some W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲).S(d)\in\mathcal{W}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{$S(d)$ contains some $W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W})$.}

Minimal winning coalitions identify the approvals sufficient to execute a proposal.

Example 2.1 (Two-out-of-three authorization).

Let N={1,2,3}N=\{1,2,3\}. For a proposed deviation dd from the baseline, S⁡(d)⊆NS(d)\subseteq N denotes the reviewers who approve it. Under two-out-of-three authorization,

𝒲={{1,2},{1,3},{2,3},N}.\mathcal{W}=\bigl\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},N\bigr\}.

Thus dd is executed exactly when S⁡(d)∈𝒲S(d)\in\mathcal{W}, or equivalently when at least two reviewers approve. The inclusion-minimal winning sets are

ℳ⁡(𝒲)={{1,2},{1,3},{2,3}},\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W})=\bigl\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}\bigr\},

since each pair is sufficient for execution, while no singleton is.

Definition 2.6 (Soundness).

For the fixed panel, an authorization rule is sound on 𝒞\mathcal{C} if every executed d∈𝒞d\in\mathcal{C} satisfies ⟨uP,d⟩≥0\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\geq 0; that is, every executed proposal weakly improves the principal’s expected utility relative to the baseline.

2.3 Coalitional coverage and coalitional alignment

An individually aligned reviewer can certify safety on its own: whenever it approves, the principal’s gain is also nonnegative. We seek a condition under which several reviewers can provide this guarantee together, even if none can provide it alone. This requires relating the principal’s utility to a nonnegative combination of their utilities. The relation need not be an exact equality, since a difference that is nonnegative on every feasible deviation can only improve the principal’s guarantee. We describe these allowable differences using the dual cone.

Definition 2.7 (Dual cone).

The dual cone of the feasible proposal cone is

𝒞∗:={z∈ℝΩ:⟨z,d⟩≥0​ for every ​d∈𝒞}.\mathcal{C}^{*}:=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}:\left\langle z,d\right\rangle\geq 0\text{ for every }d\in\mathcal{C}\}.

We now introduce our main coverage condition:

Definition 2.8 (Coalitional coverage relative to 𝒞\mathcal{C}).

A coalition S⊆NS\subseteq N covers the principal relative to 𝒞\mathcal{C} if

uP∈cone⁡{ui:i∈S}+𝒞∗.u_{P}\in\operatorname{cone}\{u_{i}:i\in S\}+\mathcal{C}^{*}.

Equivalently, there exist coefficients λi≥0\lambda_{i}\geq 0 and a vector z∈𝒞∗z\in\mathcal{C}^{*} such that

uP=∑i∈Sλi​ui+z.u_{P}=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}u_{i}+z.

To gain intuition for this definition, suppose uP=∑i∈Sλi​ui+zu_{P}=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}u_{i}+z, where each λi≥0\lambda_{i}\geq 0 and z∈𝒞∗z\in\mathcal{C}^{*}. If every reviewer in SS approves a feasible deviation dd, then

⟨uP,d⟩=∑i∈Sλi​⟨ui,d⟩+⟨z,d⟩≥0.\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle+\left\langle z,d\right\rangle\geq 0.

Thus, coverage implies soundness under the unanimous approval rule. Our characterization will show the reverse implication as well. The dual-cone term contributes a nonnegative gain on every feasible deviation. This allows the principal’s utility to differ from the reviewers’ weighted utility while preserving soundness under unanimous approval.

For a threshold rule that permits some disapprovals, soundness must follow from the reviewers who approve. Coverage must therefore survive the removal of those who disapprove, which motivates the following robust form of coalitional alignment.

Definition 2.9 (kk-robust coalitional alignment).

Adopt the convention cone⁡(∅)={0}\operatorname{cone}(\varnothing)=\{0\}. For k∈{0,…,n}k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}, the panel is kk-robustly coalitionally aligned relative to 𝒞\mathcal{C} if

uP∈cone⁡{ui:i∈S}+𝒞∗for every ​S⊆N​ with ​|S|=n−k.u_{P}\in\operatorname{cone}\{u_{i}:i\in S\}+\mathcal{C}^{*}\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq N\text{ with }|S|=n-k.

Because coverage is preserved when reviewers are added, this is equivalent to coverage by every coalition remaining after deletion of at most kk reviewers.

3 Sound authorization and rejection depth

We have seen that coalitional coverage guarantees safety when every member of a coalition approves. A general authorization rule can accept proposals without unanimous approval, so we need to determine which coalitions must provide this guarantee and whether coverage is necessary. We first study these questions through the rule’s minimal winning coalitions. We then specialize to threshold rules, where soundness depends on the fewest objections a harmful proposal can receive.

3.1 Soundness under general authorization rules

A simple example shows why a coalition can protect the principal when its members cannot do so individually. Suppose two reviewers care about different dimensions of an outcome, and the principal’s utility is the sum of theirs. A harmful proposal must then reduce at least one reviewer’s utility, so requiring both approvals guarantees soundness. Either reviewer alone may nevertheless approve a proposal whose gain in one dimension is outweighed by its loss in the other. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting difference between unanimous review and review by one member of the panel.

The example suggests examining the proposals approved unanimously by each coalition. Such approvals guarantee safety exactly when the coalition covers the principal. The following theorem relates this condition to soundness of an authorization rule, giving an exact characterization for monotone rules.

Theorem 1 (Coalitional coverage and soundness).

Let 𝒲\mathcal{W} be any authorization rule. Conditions (ii) and (iii) below are equivalent, and each implies soundness (i). If 𝒲\mathcal{W} is monotone, all three conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    𝒲\mathcal{W} is sound.

  2. (ii)

    For every minimally winning coalition W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲)W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}), the cone of feasible deviations approved by all members of WW lies in the principal’s acceptable halfspace:

    𝒞∩⋂i∈W{d:⟨ui,d⟩≥0}⊆{d:⟨uP,d⟩≥0}.\mathcal{C}\cap\bigcap_{i\in W}\{d:\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle\geq 0\}\subseteq\{d:\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\geq 0\}.
  3. (iii)

    Every minimally winning coalition covers the principal relative to 𝒞\mathcal{C}:

    uP∈cone⁡{ui:i∈W}+𝒞∗for every ​W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲).u_{P}\in\operatorname{cone}\{u_{i}:i\in W\}+\mathcal{C}^{*}\qquad\text{for every }W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}).

Equivalently, for every W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲)W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}) there exist λiW≥0\lambda_{i}^{W}\geq 0 and zW∈𝒞∗z_{W}\in\mathcal{C}^{*} such that

uP=∑i∈WλiW​ui+zW.u_{P}=\sum_{i\in W}\lambda_{i}^{W}u_{i}+z_{W}.
Proof.

Coverage and safety for a fixed coalition. For any coalition W⊆NW\subseteq N, set

KW:=𝒞∩⋂i∈W{d:⟨ui,d⟩≥0}.K_{W}:=\mathcal{C}\cap\bigcap_{i\in W}\{d:\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle\geq 0\}.

We first establish the coalition-wise equivalence

uP∈cone{ui:i∈W}+𝒞∗⟺⟨uP,d⟩≥0 for every d∈KW.u_{P}\in\operatorname{cone}\{u_{i}:i\in W\}+\mathcal{C}^{*}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\geq 0\text{ for every }d\in K_{W}. (1)

If WW covers the principal, write uP=∑i∈Wλi​ui+zu_{P}=\sum_{i\in W}\lambda_{i}u_{i}+z with λi≥0\lambda_{i}\geq 0 and z∈𝒞∗z\in\mathcal{C}^{*}. For every d∈KWd\in K_{W},

⟨uP,d⟩=∑i∈Wλi​⟨ui,d⟩+⟨z,d⟩≥0.\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle=\sum_{i\in W}\lambda_{i}\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle+\left\langle z,d\right\rangle\geq 0.

Conversely, suppose every d∈KWd\in K_{W} has nonnegative principal gain. Because 𝒞\mathcal{C} is polyhedral (it is generated by finitely many action deviations), there are vectors a1,…,aℓa_{1},\ldots,a_{\ell} such that

𝒞={d:⟨ah,d⟩≥0 for h=1,…,ℓ}.\mathcal{C}=\{d:\left\langle a_{h},d\right\rangle\geq 0\text{ for }h=1,\ldots,\ell\}.

To search for a harmful direction approved by every member of WW, consider the linear program

minimized∈ℝΩ\displaystyle\underset{d\in\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}}{\operatorname{minimize}} ⟨uP,d⟩\displaystyle\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} ⟨ah,d⟩≥0\displaystyle\left\langle a_{h},d\right\rangle\geq 0 (h=1,…,ℓ),\displaystyle(h=1,\ldots,\ell),
⟨ui,d⟩≥0\displaystyle\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle\geq 0 (i∈W).\displaystyle(i\in W).

Its feasible set is KWK_{W}, so its optimal value is zero: the objective is nonnegative on KWK_{W}, and d=0d=0 is feasible. Its LP dual is

maximizeα,λ\displaystyle\underset{\alpha,\lambda}{\operatorname{maximize}} 0\displaystyle 0
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} uP=∑h=1ℓαh​ah+∑i∈Wλi​ui,\displaystyle u_{P}=\sum_{h=1}^{\ell}\alpha_{h}a_{h}+\sum_{i\in W}\lambda_{i}u_{i},
α∈ℝ+ℓ,λ∈ℝ+W.\displaystyle\alpha\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\ell},\quad\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{W}.

Since the primal is feasible with finite optimum, LP strong duality guarantees that such multipliers exist. Each aha_{h} belongs to 𝒞∗\mathcal{C}^{*}, so z:=∑h=1ℓαh​ahz:=\sum_{h=1}^{\ell}\alpha_{h}a_{h} also belongs to 𝒞∗\mathcal{C}^{*}. The dual equality therefore gives a coverage certificate for WW. Applying this equivalence to each minimally winning coalition proves (ii)⟺\Longleftrightarrow(iii).

From coalitions to authorization rules. If (ii) holds and a proposal is executed, its approval set contains some W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲)W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}); its deviation belongs to KWK_{W}, so its principal gain is nonnegative. Hence (ii)⟹\Longrightarrow(i) for any rule.

Conversely, suppose the rule is monotone and sound. For any W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲)W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}) and d∈KWd\in K_{W}, W⊆S⁡(d)W\subseteq S(d); monotonicity makes S⁡(d)S(d) winning, and soundness gives ⟨uP,d⟩≥0\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\geq 0. Thus KWK_{W} lies in the principal’s acceptable halfspace, which is (ii). ∎

Monotonicity is needed only for the converse. A nonmonotone rule may use the disapprovals outside an accepted set as additional information, so soundness need not force that set’s approvals alone to certify safety.

Because every admissible rule (N∈𝒲N\in\mathcal{W}) executes under unanimous approval, full-panel coverage is the minimum requirement for safe delegation of any form.

Corollary 1 (Existence of an admissible sound rule).

An admissible sound authorization rule, not necessarily monotone, exists if and only if the full panel covers the principal relative to 𝒞\mathcal{C}. When this condition holds, unanimity is sound.

Proof.

If the full panel covers the principal, unanimity is sound by Theorem 1. Conversely, every admissible rule executes under unanimous approval. Soundness therefore makes every deviation approved by all reviewers principal-acceptable, so equivalence (1) gives full-panel coverage. ∎

The characterization also gives a way to construct counterexamples to soundness. If a minimally winning coalition WW fails to cover the principal, equivalence (1) gives a direction d∈𝒞d\in\mathcal{C} such that

⟨ui,d⟩≥0∀i∈W,⟨uP,d⟩<0.\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle\geq 0\quad\forall i\in W,\qquad\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle<0.

Since 𝒞=cone⁡(𝒟)\mathcal{C}=\operatorname{cone}(\mathcal{D}), a sufficiently small positive multiple of dd belongs to 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Scaling preserves the signs of all utility gains, so this gives a feasible proposal that every member of WW approves but that harms the principal. If the rule is monotone, it executes this proposal even if reviewers outside WW also approve. For each fixed coalition WW, linear programming can find either coefficients certifying coverage or such a harmful proposal.

The same characterization also answers a design question: for a fixed panel, how permissive can a sound monotone authorization rule be?

Definition 3.1 (Maximally permissive sound approval sets).

Define

𝒲sndmax:={S⊆N:uP∈cone⁡{ui:i∈S}+𝒞∗}.\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{snd}}^{\max}:=\left\{S\subseteq N:u_{P}\in\operatorname{cone}\{u_{i}:i\in S\}+\mathcal{C}^{*}\right\}.

Thus an approval set belongs to 𝒲sndmax\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{snd}}^{\max} exactly when its members’ approvals alone certify nonnegative principal gain on every feasible proposal.

Proposition 1 (Maximally permissive sound monotone rule).

If the full panel covers the principal, then 𝒲sndmax\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{snd}}^{\max} is a sound monotone authorization rule. Every sound monotone rule 𝒲\mathcal{W} satisfies

𝒲⊆𝒲sndmax.\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{snd}}^{\max}.

More generally, any family contained in 𝒲sndmax\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{snd}}^{\max} is sound; if it contains NN, it is an admissible authorization rule.

Proof.

Coverage is preserved when reviewers are added, so 𝒲sndmax\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{snd}}^{\max} is upward closed; full-panel coverage ensures that it contains NN. If S⁡(d)∈𝒲sndmaxS(d)\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{snd}}^{\max}, write

uP=∑i∈S⁡(d)λi​ui+z,λi≥0,z∈𝒞∗.u_{P}=\sum_{i\in S(d)}\lambda_{i}u_{i}+z,\qquad\lambda_{i}\geq 0,\quad z\in\mathcal{C}^{*}.

Every reviewer in S⁡(d)S(d) has nonnegative gain and ⟨z,d⟩≥0\left\langle z,d\right\rangle\geq 0, so ⟨uP,d⟩≥0\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\geq 0. This proves soundness, as well as soundness of every subfamily. Conversely, Theorem 1 says that every minimally winning coalition of a sound monotone rule covers the principal. Every winning coalition contains such a coalition and therefore covers as well, proving the inclusion. ∎

Exact coverage excludes approval of any action that results in even tiny principal loss. If the principal’s utility differs slightly from a covering combination, the same argument can bound the loss rather than rule it out. We formalize this relaxation by allowing a residual whose value on any feasible proposal is no smaller than −ε-\varepsilon.

Definition 3.2 (Approximate soundness and lower coverage).

For ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0, a rule is ε\varepsilon-sound on 𝒟\mathcal{D} if every executed d∈𝒟d\in\mathcal{D} satisfies ⟨uP,d⟩≥−ε\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\geq-\varepsilon. Define the lower residual set

ℛε−​(𝒟):={r∈ℝΩ:⟨r,d⟩≥−ε​ for every ​d∈𝒟}.\mathcal{R}^{-}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{D}):=\left\{r\in\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}:\left\langle r,d\right\rangle\geq-\varepsilon\text{ for every }d\in\mathcal{D}\right\}.

A coalition SS ε\varepsilon-covers the principal from below on 𝒟\mathcal{D} if

uP∈cone⁡{ui:i∈S}+ℛε−​(𝒟).u_{P}\in\operatorname{cone}\{u_{i}:i\in S\}+\mathcal{R}^{-}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{D}).

The panel has kk-robust lower coalitional alignment on 𝒟\mathcal{D} at tolerance ε\varepsilon if every coalition of n−kn-k reviewers has this property. Equivalently, every coalition of at least n−kn-k reviewers does.

We state exact results on the scale-free cone 𝒞\mathcal{C} and nonzero error bounds on 𝒟\mathcal{D}, because the magnitude of an approximation error depends on scale. These parameters do not alter sincere voting: reviewers still approve exactly when their own gain is nonnegative. Appendix A gives the approximate counterpart of Theorem 1.

3.2 Threshold voting and rejection depth

We now specialize the characterization to threshold rules, which decide whether to execute a proposal using only the number of disapprovals. Because these rules treat reviewers symmetrically, their minimal winning coalitions are determined by a single count. The question is how many disapprovals the rule can tolerate while still rejecting every harmful proposal. This is determined by the harmful proposal that receives the fewest objections, which motivates the following definition of rejection depth.

Definition 3.3 (Threshold rule and rejection depth).

For k∈{0,…,n−1}k\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}, the kk-tolerant threshold rule executes a proposal when at most kk reviewers disapprove. Write

N−​(d):={i∈N:⟨ui,d⟩<0}N^{-}(d):=\{i\in N:\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle<0\}

for the reviewers who disapprove deviation dd. The rejection depth of the principal relative to the panel is the fewest objections received by any harmful feasible direction:

depth𝒞⁡(uP,u1,…,un):=mind∈𝒞⟨uP,d⟩<0⁡|N−​(d)|.\operatorname{depth}_{\mathcal{C}}(u_{P};u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}):=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\in\mathcal{C}\\ \left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle<0\end{subarray}}|N^{-}(d)|.

See Figure 2 for a visualization. If the principal has no harmful feasible direction, set the depth equal to n+1n+1.

Thus a kk-tolerant rule is sound exactly when every harmful feasible proposal receives at least k+1k+1 objections. Its minimal winning coalitions are all sets of n−kn-k reviewers, so Theorem 1 gives an equivalent condition: coverage must survive the deletion of any kk reviewers. Rejection depth and robust coalitional alignment therefore express the same requirement, one by counting objections and the other by relating the reviewers’ utilities to the principal’s.

Corollary 2 (Coalitional alignment characterizes threshold soundness).

For every k∈{0,…,n−1}k\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}, the following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    the kk-tolerant threshold rule is sound;

  2. (ii)

    depth𝒞⁡(uP,u1,…,un)≥k+1\operatorname{depth}_{\mathcal{C}}(u_{P};u_{1},\ldots,u_{n})\geq k+1;

  3. (iii)

    the panel is kk-robustly coalitionally aligned relative to 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

More generally, the rule is εharm\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}-sound on 𝒟\mathcal{D} if and only if the panel has kk-robust lower coalitional alignment on 𝒟\mathcal{D} at tolerance εharm\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}.

Proof.

The rule executes exactly when |N−​(d)|≤k|N^{-}(d)|\leq k. It is therefore sound exactly when every harmful deviation has |N−​(d)|≥k+1|N^{-}(d)|\geq k+1, proving (i)⟺\Longleftrightarrow(ii). Its minimally winning coalitions are the (n−k)(n-k)-element sets, so Theorem 1 turns the same condition into (iii). Replacing exact coverage by lower coverage and using Theorem 5 (Appendix A) proves the approximate statement. ∎

3.3 How robust coalitional alignment can arise

We close the static analysis with a simple way in which coalitional alignment can arise from reviewer heterogeneity. Suppose reviewers are sampled independently and their misalignment directions are centrally symmetric around the principal’s objective. Informally, this models a setting in which alignment is hard because when attempting to produce an aligned agent, their realized utility function is noisy (perhaps very noisy), but not systematically biased. Then every harmful direction is opposed by at least half the population. Uniform convergence makes the same statement hold, up to a vanishing error, for a sufficiently large sampled panel.

Corollary 3 (Centrally symmetric objective noise).

Suppose the reviewer objectives are drawn independently and identically as ui=uP+ξiu_{i}=u_{P}+\xi_{i}, and every one-dimensional projection ⟨ξi,d⟩\left\langle\xi_{i},d\right\rangle is centrally symmetric about zero. In fixed feasible dimension,

1n​depth𝒞​(uP,u1,…,un)≥12−o⁡(1)\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{depth}_{\mathcal{C}}(u_{P};u_{1},\ldots,u_{n})\geq\frac{1}{2}-o(1)

with high probability as n→∞n\to\infty.

If the population assigns probability zero to the principal’s positive utility ray on the feasible span, then almost surely no sampled reviewer is individually aligned. Nevertheless, for fixed feasible dimension the panel soundly tolerates deletion of nearly half its reviewers with high probability as nn grows. Appendix A gives the finite-sample bound, a more general population condition, and the proof.

4 Sequential authorization in a discounted MDP

The one-decision model evaluates a proposal in isolation. For a long-running agent, authorization instead takes place repeatedly: each executed action changes the state from which the next proposal will be made. A reviewer must therefore account for the action’s future consequences as well as its immediate reward. We extend the model to a discounted MDP and replace the baseline action with a baseline policy. This policy specifies what to do after rejection and provides a common continuation against which each participant evaluates a proposed action.

4.1 Control model and continuation-aware votes

Definition 4.1 (Discounted control model).

Consider a finite discounted MDP with state space 𝒮\mathcal{S}, action space AA, transition kernel 𝖯\mathsf{P}, and discount factor γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Participant j∈{P,1,…,n}j\in\{P,1,\ldots,n\} has bounded reward function rj​(s,a)r_{j}(s,a). Fix a stationary randomized baseline policy π0\pi^{0}. Participant jj’s baseline value and action-value functions are

Vj0​(s)\displaystyle V_{j}^{0}(s) :=𝔼π0​[∑t=0∞γt​rj​(st,at)|s0=s],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{0}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{j}(s_{t},a_{t})\,\middle|\,s_{0}=s\right],
Qj0​(s,a)\displaystyle Q_{j}^{0}(s,a) :=rj(s,a)+γ𝔼s′∼𝖯(⋅∣s,a)[Vj0(s′)],\displaystyle:=r_{j}(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim\mathsf{P}(\cdot\mid s,a)}[V_{j}^{0}(s^{\prime})],

respectively.

These two value functions compare continuations from the same state. Vj0​(s)V_{j}^{0}(s) is participant jj’s expected discounted reward from following the baseline policy starting at ss. In Qj0​(s,a)Q_{j}^{0}(s,a), only the first action changes: action aa is taken at ss and the baseline is followed thereafter. Their difference measures how this one-step deviation changes the participant’s long-run reward, and is called the baseline advantage:

The use of QQ-values rather than immediate rewards is essential. Two actions can have the same reward at the current state while sending the system to states with very different future value. A reviewer voting from ri​(s,a)r_{i}(s,a) alone would miss this effect; Qi0​(s,a)Q_{i}^{0}(s,a) evaluates the complete deviation consisting of the proposed action followed by the baseline continuation.

Reviewers therefore need access to their baseline-continuation values, or estimates of them; Appendix D bounds the effect of errors in those evaluations.

Definition 4.2 (Continuation-aware authorization).

At state ss, the proposer agent selects a randomized action q∈𝒬s⊆Δ⁡(A)q\in\mathcal{Q}_{s}\subseteq\Delta(A), where 𝒬s\mathcal{Q}_{s} is a convex polytope containing π0(⋅∣s)\pi^{0}(\cdot\mid s). Reviewer ii approves when the proposed one-step deviation, followed conceptually by the baseline continuation, weakly improves their value:

∑aq⁡(a)​Qi0​(s,a)\displaystyle\sum_{a}q(a)Q_{i}^{0}(s,a) ≥Vi0​(s)\displaystyle\geq V_{i}^{0}(s)
=∑aπ0​(a∣s)​Qi0​(s,a).\displaystyle=\sum_{a}\pi^{0}(a\mid s)Q_{i}^{0}(s,a).

Equivalently,

⟨Qi0(s,⋅),q−π0(⋅∣s)⟩≥0.\left\langle Q_{i}^{0}(s,\cdot),q-\pi^{0}(\cdot\mid s)\right\rangle\geq 0.

Write

Ss(q):={i∈N:⟨Qi0(s,⋅),q−π0(⋅∣s)⟩≥0}S_{s}(q):=\left\{i\in N:\left\langle Q_{i}^{0}(s,\cdot),q-\pi^{0}(\cdot\mid s)\right\rangle\geq 0\right\}

for the approval set at state ss. A state-dependent authorization rule specifies a family 𝒲s⊆2N\mathcal{W}_{s}\subseteq 2^{N} with N∈𝒲sN\in\mathcal{W}_{s} at each state. It executes qq when Ss​(q)∈𝒲sS_{s}(q)\in\mathcal{W}_{s}. If the proposal is rejected, the rule instead samples an action from π0(⋅∣s)\pi^{0}(\cdot\mid s). The rule uses the state to select 𝒲s\mathcal{W}_{s} and receives one bit from each reviewer. It is monotone if each family 𝒲s\mathcal{W}_{s} is upward closed.

The statewise deviation set and cone are

𝒟s\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{s} :={q−π0(⋅∣s):q∈𝒬s},\displaystyle:=\{q-\pi^{0}(\cdot\mid s):q\in\mathcal{Q}_{s}\},
𝒞s\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{s} :=cone⁡(𝒟s).\displaystyle:=\operatorname{cone}(\mathcal{D}_{s}).

Because 𝒬s\mathcal{Q}_{s} is a polytope, 𝒞s\mathcal{C}_{s} is a polyhedral cone. The baseline QQ-vectors Qj0​(s,⋅)Q_{j}^{0}(s,\cdot) are the analogue of the utility vectors in the static setting.

The proposer agent need not follow a stationary or Markov policy. At every time it may choose its proposal as an arbitrary function of the entire observed history. The authorization layer is thus required to protect the principal against adaptive sequences of individually reviewed actions, not merely against a fixed candidate policy.

4.2 From local authorization to global control

The static characterization applies at each state with the baseline QQ-vectors as utilities, but the guarantee it gives concerns a particular continuation: take the proposed action once and then follow the baseline. The actual process need not follow that continuation. After the action is executed, the proposer agent observes the new state and may submit another proposal, possibly in response to the entire history. Figure 3 illustrates the difference between the comparison used to cast a vote and the trajectory that results from repeated authorization. We need to show that safety of each local comparison protects the principal along this adaptive trajectory.

The next theorem establishes the equivalence of the local condition (i) with the global guarantee (ii); for monotone rules, the local condition has the same coalitional coverage form as in the static analysis.

Theorem 2 (Local soundness characterizes baseline safety).

Fix state-dependent authorization rules (𝒲s)s∈𝒮(\mathcal{W}_{s})_{s\in\mathcal{S}}, not necessarily monotone. The following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    At every state ss, every proposal q∈𝒬sq\in\mathcal{Q}_{s} that the rule executes has nonnegative principal baseline advantage:

    ⟨QP0(s,⋅),q−π0(⋅∣s)⟩≥0.\left\langle Q_{P}^{0}(s,\cdot),q-\pi^{0}(\cdot\mid s)\right\rangle\geq 0.
  2. (ii)

    For every initial state s0s_{0} and every proposer agent whose proposals may depend arbitrarily on the full interaction history, the resulting history-dependent policy π\pi satisfies

    JP​(π∣s0)≥VP0​(s0),J_{P}(\pi\mid s_{0})\geq V_{P}^{0}(s_{0}),

    where

    JP​(π∣s0):=𝔼π​[∑t=0∞γt​rP​(st,at)|s0].J_{P}(\pi\mid s_{0}):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{P}(s_{t},a_{t})\,\middle|\,s_{0}\right].

If each 𝒲s\mathcal{W}_{s} is monotone, these conditions are further equivalent to statewise coalitional coverage: at every state ss and for every W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲s)W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}_{s}),

QP0​(s,⋅)∈cone⁡{Qi0​(s,⋅):i∈W}+𝒞s∗.Q_{P}^{0}(s,\cdot)\in\operatorname{cone}\{Q_{i}^{0}(s,\cdot):i\in W\}+\mathcal{C}_{s}^{*}.

The reason local safety suffices is the performance-difference identity. It expresses the principal’s expected gain over the baseline as the expected discounted sum of baseline advantages along the actual trajectory. Conditional on any observed history, local soundness makes the advantage of an authorized proposal nonnegative in expectation; choosing the baseline after rejection contributes zero. Summing these quantities gives the global guarantee even when future proposals adapt to earlier outcomes. Conversely, if local soundness fails at one state, a proposer starting there can submit the harmful proposal once and then return to the baseline. The resulting loss shows why the local condition is also necessary.

If local soundness holds only up to an error, the same identity bounds the accumulated loss. Each state’s error contributes in proportion to how often that state is visited and how far into the future it is reached.

Corollary 4 (Approximate local losses compose globally).

Fix a function εharm:𝒮→[0,∞)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}:\mathcal{S}\to[0,\infty). For monotone rules, the statewise guarantee that every executed proposal at ss has principal baseline advantage at least −εharm​(s)-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}(s) is equivalent to

QP0​(s,⋅)∈cone⁡{Qi0​(s,⋅):i∈W}+ℛεharm​(s)−​(𝒟s)for every ​W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲s).Q_{P}^{0}(s,\cdot)\in\operatorname{cone}\{Q_{i}^{0}(s,\cdot):i\in W\}+\mathcal{R}^{-}_{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}(s)}(\mathcal{D}_{s})\qquad\text{for every }W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}_{s}).

For rules of any form, these local bounds imply

JP​(π∣s0)−VP0​(s0)≥−𝔼π​[∑t=0∞γt​εharm​(st)|s0].J_{P}(\pi\mid s_{0})-V_{P}^{0}(s_{0})\geq-\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}(s_{t})\,\middle|\,s_{0}\right].

In particular, a uniform bound εharm​(s)≤ε¯harm\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}(s)\leq\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{harm}} gives

JP​(π∣s0)≥VP0​(s0)−ε¯harm1−γ.J_{P}(\pi\mid s_{0})\geq V_{P}^{0}(s_{0})-\frac{\bar{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{harm}}}{1-\gamma}.
Proof of Theorem 2 and Corollary 4.

Local bounds imply global bounds. Consider first the general local bound in the corollary; the exact implication is the special case εharm≡0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}\equiv 0. For an executed proposal qq at state ss, the identity

∑aπ0​(a∣s)​QP0​(s,a)=VP0​(s),\sum_{a}\pi^{0}(a\mid s)Q_{P}^{0}(s,a)=V_{P}^{0}(s),

shows that a local principal-gain bound −εharm​(s)-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}(s) is equivalent to

∑aq⁡(a)​AP0​(s,a)≥−εharm​(s).\sum_{a}q(a)A_{P}^{0}(s,a)\geq-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}(s).

A rejected proposal causes the rule to use π0(⋅∣s)\pi^{0}(\cdot\mid s), whose expected baseline advantage is exactly zero. Hence, conditional on every history hth_{t},

𝔼π​[AP0​(st,at)∣ht]≥−εharm​(st).\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[A_{P}^{0}(s_{t},a_{t})\mid h_{t}]\geq-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}(s_{t}).

For every finite TT, the Bellman equation for VP0V_{P}^{0} telescopes to the performance-difference identity (Kakade and Langford, 2002)

𝔼π​[∑t=0Tγt​AP0​(st,at)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}A_{P}^{0}(s_{t},a_{t})\right] =𝔼π​[∑t=0Tγt​rP​(st,at)]−VP0​(s0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}r_{P}(s_{t},a_{t})\right]-V_{P}^{0}(s_{0})
+γT+1​𝔼π​[VP0​(sT+1)].\displaystyle\qquad+\gamma^{T+1}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[V_{P}^{0}(s_{T+1})].

Since rewards and VP0V_{P}^{0} are bounded, the final term vanishes as T→∞T\to\infty. Therefore

JP​(π∣s0)−VP0​(s0)=𝔼π​[∑t=0∞γt​AP0​(st,at)].J_{P}(\pi\mid s_{0})-V_{P}^{0}(s_{0})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}A_{P}^{0}(s_{t},a_{t})\right].

Iterated expectation now gives

JP​(π∣s0)−VP0​(s0)≥−𝔼π​[∑t=0∞γt​εharm​(st)|s0].J_{P}(\pi\mid s_{0})-V_{P}^{0}(s_{0})\geq-\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}(s_{t})\,\middle|\,s_{0}\right].

Taking εharm≡0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}\equiv 0 proves (i)⟹\Longrightarrow(ii), and a uniform bound is summed by the geometric series. This proves the corollary’s quantitative claims.

Global bounds force local soundness. Suppose (i) fails at some state ss. Then an executed proposal q∈𝒬sq\in\mathcal{Q}_{s} satisfies

⟨QP0(s,⋅),q−π0(⋅∣s)⟩<0.\left\langle Q_{P}^{0}(s,\cdot),q-\pi^{0}(\cdot\mid s)\right\rangle<0.

Starting from ss, let the proposer agent submit this proposal once and submit the baseline distribution thereafter. The resulting policy has negative expected baseline advantage at time zero and zero expected baseline advantage at every later time. The performance-difference identity therefore gives

JP​(π∣s)<VP0​(s),J_{P}(\pi\mid s)<V_{P}^{0}(s),

contradicting (ii). Hence (ii) implies (i).

Finally, for monotone rules, applying Theorem 1 and Theorem 5 (Appendix A) at each state gives the two coalitional characterizations. ∎

Specializing to threshold review recovers the language of robust coalitional alignment, now applied to the baseline QQ-vectors at each state:

Corollary 5 (Threshold review in the control process).

Suppose state ss uses a ksk_{s}-tolerant threshold, where ks∈{0,…,n−1}k_{s}\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}. The following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    for every initial state s0s_{0} and every history-adaptive proposer agent, the resulting policy π\pi satisfies JP​(π∣s0)≥VP0​(s0)J_{P}(\pi\mid s_{0})\geq V_{P}^{0}(s_{0});

  2. (ii)

    at every state ss, the panel is ksk_{s}-robustly coalitionally aligned relative to 𝒞s\mathcal{C}_{s} when participant utilities are the vectors Qj0​(s,⋅)Q_{j}^{0}(s,\cdot).

More generally, for any function εharm:𝒮→[0,∞)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}:\mathcal{S}\to[0,\infty), if the baseline QQ-vectors have ksk_{s}-robust lower coalitional alignment on 𝒟s\mathcal{D}_{s} at tolerance εharm​(s)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}(s), then the quantitative welfare bound in Corollary 4 holds.

Proof.

Apply Corollary 2 at each state and then Theorem 2. ∎

4.3 A state-independent certificate from reward functions

For monotone authorization rules, Theorem 2 characterizes safety through coverage by the baseline QQ-vectors at every state; without monotonicity, coverage remains sufficient. Because these vectors depend on the transition kernel and baseline policy, a separate certificate may be needed at each state. We therefore look for a stronger sufficient condition that can be checked directly on the reward functions, before choosing a baseline policy or computing any continuation values.

Definition 4.3 (Reward-function coverage).

A coalition SS covers the principal in reward-function space if there are coefficients λiS≥0\lambda_{i}^{S}\geq 0 such that

rP​(s,a)=∑i∈SλiS​ri​(s,a)for every ​(s,a)∈𝒮×A.r_{P}(s,a)=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}^{S}r_{i}(s,a)\qquad\text{for every }(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times A.

The coefficients in this definition are fixed across states and actions. Discounted sums and expectations preserve the equality, so the same coefficients also combine the reviewers’ baseline QQ-values into the principal’s. This condition is stronger than statewise coverage, but supplies it at every state and for every choice of dynamics.

Corollary 6 (Reward-function coverage lifts to every state).

Fix an authorization rule 𝒲\mathcal{W}, not necessarily monotone. Suppose every inclusion-minimal winning approval set covers the principal in reward-function space. Then, for every transition kernel, baseline policy, initial state, and history-adaptive proposer agent, the same state-independent rule 𝒲\mathcal{W} keeps the principal’s expected discounted utility at least as high as under the baseline.

In particular, the state-independent kk-tolerant threshold rule has this guarantee if every (n−k)(n-k)-reviewer coalition covers the principal in reward-function space.

Proof.

Fix a reward-function certificate for SS. Linearity of expectation under the baseline gives

VP0​(s)=∑i∈SλiS​Vi0​(s)andQP0​(s,a)=∑i∈SλiS​Qi0​(s,a)V_{P}^{0}(s)=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}^{S}V_{i}^{0}(s)\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q_{P}^{0}(s,a)=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}^{S}Q_{i}^{0}(s,a)

for every state ss and action aa. Thus SS has a zero-slack statewise QQ-vector cover. Every winning approval set contains an inclusion-minimal winning subset, and coverage is preserved when reviewers are added. Thus every winning approval set has a zero-slack statewise QQ-vector cover, and Theorem 2 gives the claimed baseline-safety guarantee. For the threshold rule, every winning set contains an (n−k)(n-k)-element covering subset, proving the final claim. ∎

The reward identity in Corollary 6 gives a guarantee that holds for every choice of dynamics. For a fixed transition kernel, however, equality of reward functions is stronger than needed: authorization depends on comparisons with the baseline. Discounted potential-based shaping can change the rewards while leaving every baseline advantage and every policy’s return relative to the baseline unchanged (Ng et al., 1999). Appendix B.1 characterizes the resulting relaxation of reward-function coverage.

5 Strategic reviewers and the role of unanimity

The preceding guarantees allow reviewers to have different objectives but assume that they report their comparisons sincerely. A reviewer acting to maximize its own return may instead have an incentive to vote insincerely, especially when its vote affects which proposals it will face later. We now ask when authorization remains safe under this strategic behavior. We begin with a single decision, where the reviewer’s incentive depends on whether its vote can change the outcome and on the sign of its gain from execution. We then return to the control process.

Sincere voting in one decision.

Fix a single feasible proposal with deviation d∈𝒟d\in\mathcal{D}. Normalize every reviewer’s payoff from rejection to zero, so reviewer ii receives ⟨ui,d⟩\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle if the proposal is executed. The reviewers vote simultaneously, and the authorization rule maps their approval set to execution or rejection. Under a monotone rule, sincerity is weakly dominant: a reviewer can change the outcome only toward execution by approving, or toward rejection by disapproving.

Proposition 2 (Sincere voting is weakly dominant).

Fix a proposal dd and a monotone authorization rule. If ⟨ui,d⟩>0\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle>0, approving weakly dominates disapproving for reviewer ii; if ⟨ui,d⟩<0\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle<0, disapproving weakly dominates approving. If ⟨ui,d⟩=0\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle=0, both votes are optimal. Consequently, the sincere voting profile is a dominant-strategy equilibrium of the one-decision game.

Proof.

Fix the other reviewers’ votes. By monotonicity, changing reviewer ii’s vote from disapproval to approval either leaves the outcome unchanged or changes it from rejection to execution. The latter change gives reviewer ii gain ⟨ui,d⟩\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle. Its sign determines the weakly dominant vote; when the gain is zero, the reviewer is indifferent. ∎

Weak dominance does not eliminate all Nash equilibria: a reviewer may vote insincerely whenever its vote cannot change the outcome. Appendix B.2 shows that the ability to force rejection alone exactly characterizes one-decision Nash safety and records the refinement obtained by excluding weakly dominated votes. To describe who can force rejection, we distinguish individual veto power from the ability of several reviewers to block a proposal together.

For a monotone rule, a coalition B⊆NB\subseteq N is blocking if N∖B∉𝒲N\setminus B\notin\mathcal{W}: unanimous disapproval by its members forces rejection, regardless of the votes outside BB. Let ℬ⁡(𝒲)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{W}) be the set of inclusion-minimal blocking coalitions. A reviewer has veto power if it can force rejection alone, and the set of veto reviewers is

V⁡(𝒲):={i∈N:N∖{i}∉𝒲}.V(\mathcal{W}):=\{i\in N:N\setminus\{i\}\notin\mathcal{W}\}.

5.1 Strategic safety in the control process

In the control process, a reviewer’s vote today shapes the proposals it will face tomorrow, so sincere statewise comparison is no longer dominant and we must work with equilibrium behavior directly. Return to the discounted MDP of Section 4. Fix any possibly randomized, history-dependent proposer policy ρ\rho. A review policy σi\sigma_{i} maps the observed history and current proposal to a possibly randomized vote. For a profile σ=(σ1,…,σn)\sigma=(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n}), let

Jj​(ρ,σ∣s0):=𝔼ρ,σ​[∑t=0∞γt​rj​(st,at)|s0]J_{j}(\rho,\sigma\mid s_{0}):=\mathbb{E}_{\rho,\sigma}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{j}(s_{t},a_{t})\,\middle|\,s_{0}\right]

be participant jj’s expected return along the trajectory actually induced by the proposer, the votes, and the fallback to the baseline after rejection. Reviewer ii chooses σi\sigma_{i} to maximize JiJ_{i}. Thus the strategic objective is the realized continuation payoff, not the baseline-QQ comparison that defines a sincere vote.

Under unanimity, a reviewer can secure its baseline return by always disapproving. A threshold that tolerates kk disapprovals requires k+1k+1 reviewers to act together to force the baseline. We therefore consider stability against joint deviations, as well as deviations by one reviewer.

Definition 5.1 (Coalitional stability).

Fix a proposer policy ρ\rho, an initial state s0s_{0}, an integer c≥1c\geq 1 and reviewer-specific tolerances 𝜼=(η1,…,ηn)∈ℝ+n\boldsymbol{\eta}=(\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{n})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}. A review-policy profile is (c,𝛈)(c,\boldsymbol{\eta})-coalitionally stable if no coalition BB with 1≤|B|≤c1\leq|B|\leq c has a joint deviation in its review policies that raises each member ii’s return by more than ηi\eta_{i}, holding the proposer and all other review policies fixed. We abbreviate (c,𝟎)(c,\boldsymbol{0})-coalitional stability as cc-coalitional stability.

1-coalitional stability is ordinary Nash equilibrium in the reviewer game; nn-coalitional stability is strong Nash equilibrium (Aumann, 1959). Although related in spirit to the cooperative-game core (Gillies, 1959), cc-coalitional stability is distinct: the core asks whether any coalition can secure an alternative outcome that all its members prefer, whereas our notion asks whether a coalition of at most cc reviewers can all benefit by jointly changing their voting policies within the fixed authorization game. Our definition is weaker than the cc-resilient equilibrium used in distributed game theory, which rules out a coalition deviation that benefits even one deviating member (Abraham et al., 2006). If the proposer agent is itself strategic, the reviewer component of any Nash equilibrium of the full game is 1-coalitionally stable conditional on the proposer’s equilibrium strategy.

To turn coalitional stability into a guarantee for the principal, we need to relate the participants’ returns along the trajectory they actually induce. We use the stronger reward-function coverage condition from Definition 4.3. Each coalition’s covering coefficients are fixed across states and actions, so the same identity relates its members’ returns to the principal’s, including their gains over the baseline. This lets us infer from a principal loss that sufficiently many reviewers would also benefit from forcing a return to the baseline.

Theorem 3 (Coalitional stability and strategic safety).

Fix a monotone authorization rule 𝒲\mathcal{W}. Assume every minimally winning coalition W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲)W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}) covers the principal in reward-function space: there are coefficients λiW≥0\lambda_{i}^{W}\geq 0 such that

rP=∑i∈WλiW​ri.r_{P}=\sum_{i\in W}\lambda_{i}^{W}r_{i}.

Fix any proposer policy ρ\rho and initial state s0s_{0}. Suppose that, at the review-policy profile σ\sigma, no minimally blocking coalition B∈ℬ⁡(𝒲)B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{W}) can strictly improve every member’s return by jointly switching to always disapproving, holding the proposer and all other review policies fixed. Then

JP​(ρ,σ∣s0)≥VP0​(s0).J_{P}(\rho,\sigma\mid s_{0})\geq V_{P}^{0}(s_{0}).

In particular, if ℬ⁡(𝒲)≠∅\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{W})\neq\varnothing, let c:=maxB∈ℬ⁡(𝒲)⁡|B|c:=\max_{B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{W})}|B|. Every cc-coalitionally stable profile is baseline-safe. If ℬ⁡(𝒲)=∅\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{W})=\varnothing, every profile is baseline-safe. Under the kk-tolerant threshold, c=k+1c=k+1 and it is enough that every (n−k)(n-k)-reviewer coalition cover the principal in reward-function space.

Proof.

Write Δj:=Jj​(ρ,σ∣s0)−Vj0​(s0)\Delta_{j}:=J_{j}(\rho,\sigma\mid s_{0})-V_{j}^{0}(s_{0}). Because every participant’s return is evaluated along the same realized trajectory, reward-function coverage and linearity give, for every minimally winning coalition WW,

ΔP=∑i∈WλiW​Δi.\Delta_{P}=\sum_{i\in W}\lambda_{i}^{W}\Delta_{i}.

Suppose toward a contradiction that ΔP<0\Delta_{P}<0, and let S+:={i:Δi≥0}S_{+}:=\{i:\Delta_{i}\geq 0\}. This set cannot be winning: otherwise it contains some W∈ℳ⁡(𝒲)W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W}), and applying (∗)(*) to that WW would give ΔP≥0\Delta_{P}\geq 0. Hence S+S_{+} is losing, so its complement is blocking and contains some B∈ℬ⁡(𝒲)B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{W}). Every i∈Bi\in B has Δi<0\Delta_{i}<0. If the members of BB jointly always disapprove, they force every proposal to be rejected and hence force the baseline policy, strictly improving every member’s return. This contradicts the assumed stability. Therefore ΔP≥0\Delta_{P}\geq 0. ∎

Reward-function coverage ensures that if every member of a winning coalition earns at least its baseline return, then the principal does too. If the principal instead loses, the reviewers who are below baseline must therefore contain a blocking coalition. Its members can all improve by always disapproving and thereby forcing the baseline policy. Coalitional stability rules out this profitable joint deviation, and hence rules out a loss for the principal.

Remark 5.1 (Approximate coalitional stability).

In the setting of Theorem 3, fix covering coefficients λiW\lambda_{i}^{W} and let c≥1c\geq 1 be at least the size of every minimally blocking coalition. Every (c,𝜼)(c,\boldsymbol{\eta})-coalitionally stable profile satisfies

JP​(ρ,σ∣s0)−VP0​(s0)≥−max⁡∑i∈WW∈ℳ⁡(𝒲)⁡λiW​ηi.J_{P}(\rho,\sigma\mid s_{0})-V_{P}^{0}(s_{0})\geq-\max_{W\in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{W})}\sum_{i\in W}\lambda_{i}^{W}\eta_{i}.

With Δj\Delta_{j} as in the proof, set S+:={i:Δi≥−ηi}S_{+}:=\{i:\Delta_{i}\geq-\eta_{i}\}. If S+S_{+} is winning, the return identity for a minimally winning coalition it contains gives the bound. Otherwise, its complement contains a minimally blocking coalition whose members each gain more than ηi\eta_{i} by jointly forcing the baseline, contradicting stability.

Under unanimity, the joint deviation required by the theorem reduces to a deviation by one reviewer, since every reviewer can force the baseline on its own. Every reviewer therefore earns at least its baseline return at a Nash equilibrium. Full-panel reward-function coverage transfers these inequalities to the principal through a nonnegative combination. This gives a safety guarantee even in a game where the proposer agent also chooses its policy strategically.

Corollary 7 (Nash safety in the full proposer–reviewer game).

Suppose the full panel covers the principal in reward-function space. Under unanimity, every Nash equilibrium of a game in which the proposer agent and reviewers all choose history-dependent policies gives the principal expected return at least VP0​(s0)V_{P}^{0}(s_{0}), regardless of the proposer’s objective.

Proof.

Fix a Nash equilibrium and hold the proposer’s equilibrium policy fixed. The reviewers’ equilibrium policies form a Nash equilibrium in the resulting reviewer game. Under unanimity, any reviewer can force the baseline by always disapproving, so the profile satisfies the deviation condition in Theorem 3. Apply that theorem. ∎

This Nash-safety guarantee depends on unanimity. If the rule tolerates even one disapproval and everyone approves, a single reviewer cannot prevent execution by changing its vote. Suppose also that the proposer responds to past votes only through whether a proposal was executed or rejected. A unilateral change in voting then leaves future proposals unchanged as well. Consequently, always approving can remain a Nash equilibrium even when the resulting trajectory harms the principal and every reviewer would prefer the baseline.

Proposition 3 (Unsafe Nash equilibria under permissive thresholds).

Fix k∈{1,…,n−1}k\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\} and a proposer policy ρ\rho that depends on past votes only through the resulting execute/reject decisions. Let σall\sigma^{\mathrm{all}} be the profile in which every reviewer always approves. If executing every proposal made by ρ\rho yields

JP​(ρ,σall∣s0)<VP0​(s0),J_{P}(\rho,\sigma^{\mathrm{all}}\mid s_{0})<V_{P}^{0}(s_{0}),

then σall\sigma^{\mathrm{all}} is an unsafe Nash equilibrium of the reviewer game under the kk-tolerant threshold.

Proof.

A unilateral deviation can create at most one disapproval, which a kk-tolerant threshold with k≥1k\geq 1 ignores. Couple the deviating and all-approve plays using the same transition and proposer randomness. An induction over review times shows that each execute/reject decision is the same; the assumed invariance of ρ\rho then gives the same next proposal, so the entire state–action trajectory is the same. The deviator’s payoff is therefore unchanged and the all-approve profile is a Nash equilibrium. The displayed inequality makes it unsafe. ∎

The failure can occur even when all reviewers are aligned with the principal: they may all prefer the baseline while no one can force it alone. Under a kk-tolerant threshold, k+1k+1 reviewers can do so jointly. The coalitional-stability requirement in Theorem 3 rules out such an outcome, but requires more than ordinary Nash equilibrium. The guarantee for a permissive threshold therefore combines the stated coverage condition with a stronger behavioral assumption about joint deviations by blocking coalitions.

6 Completeness and the limits of binary approval

Soundness protects the principal against harmful proposals, but places no requirement on proposals that would benefit them. A panel can therefore be sound while rejecting many desirable actions. We return to sincere review in the one-decision model and ask whether an authorization rule can also execute every proposal the principal finds acceptable. This complementary requirement is completeness; together, soundness and completeness ask the rule to recover all of the decisions that the principal would themselves make from only the reviewers’ reports.

Definition 6.1 (Completeness and approximate implementation).

A rule is complete on 𝒞\mathcal{C} if it executes every d∈𝒞d\in\mathcal{C} with ⟨uP,d⟩≥0\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\geq 0. For εgood≥0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{good}}\geq 0, it is εgood\varepsilon_{\mathrm{good}}-complete on 𝒟\mathcal{D} if it executes every d∈𝒟d\in\mathcal{D} with ⟨uP,d⟩≥εgood\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\geq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{good}}. Together with εharm\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}}-soundness, this gives an (εharm,εgood)(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{harm}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{good}})-implementation. Exact soundness and completeness are the zero-error case.

6.1 The limits of binary approval

The complementary-reviewer example shows what can be lost when only binary votes are reported. Let u1=e1u_{1}=e_{1}, u2=e2u_{2}=e_{2}, and uP=e1+e2u_{P}=e_{1}+e_{2} on 𝒞=ℝ2\mathcal{C}=\mathbb{R}^{2}, as in Figure 1. The deviations (2,−1)(2,-1) and (1,−2)(1,-2) both receive approval from reviewer 1 and disapproval from reviewer 2, but their principal gains are 11 and −1-1, respectively. Any rule based on the approval set must make the same decision on both, so it either rejects the beneficial proposal or executes the harmful one. The following theorem generalizes this obstruction by examining where reviewers’ votes can change as feasible proposals cross the principal’s indifference boundary.

Theorem 4 (Binary separation and exact implementation).

Let L:=span⁡(𝒞)L:=\operatorname{span}(\mathcal{C}), and suppose there are deviations d+,d−∈𝒞d_{+},d_{-}\in\mathcal{C} such that

⟨uP,d+⟩>0and⟨uP,d−⟩<0.\left\langle u_{P},d_{+}\right\rangle>0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\langle u_{P},d_{-}\right\rangle<0.

Let f:2N→{0,1}f:2^{N}\to\{0,1\} be any deterministic rule based only on the approval set, not necessarily monotone. Suppose

⟨uP,d⟩>0⟹f(S(d))=1,⟨uP,d⟩<0⟹f(S(d))=0(d∈𝒞).\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle>0\Longrightarrow f(S(d))=1,\qquad\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle<0\Longrightarrow f(S(d))=0\qquad(d\in\mathcal{C}).

Then:

  1. (i)

    some reviewer ii has the same indifference hyperplane as the principal on feasible proposals: for some c≠0c\neq 0,

    ⟨ui,d⟩=c⁡⟨uP,d⟩for every ​d∈L;\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle=c\,\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\qquad\text{for every }d\in L;
  2. (ii)

    if ff is monotone, then some such reviewer has c>0c>0 and is aligned with the principal;

  3. (iii)

    the same positive-alignment conclusion holds, without monotonicity, if f⁡(S⁡(d))=1f(S(d))=1 whenever ⟨uP,d⟩=0\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle=0.

Thus exact soundness and completeness require an aligned reviewer even for a nonmonotone rule. The weaker task of separating only strict gains from strict losses still requires a reviewer with the correct boundary, but a nonmonotone rule could invert the vote of a negatively proportional reviewer. Monotonicity or the convention that principal indifference is accepted rules out that inversion. Appendix C gives the proof.

Corollary 8 (Exact binary implementation).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 4, a deterministic approval-set rule satisfying

f(S(d))=1⟺⟨uP,d⟩≥0(d∈𝒞)f(S(d))=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\geq 0\qquad(d\in\mathcal{C})

exists if and only if some reviewer is aligned with the principal on LL. When such a reviewer exists, its vote alone gives a monotone exact rule.

Proof.

Necessity is part (iii) of Theorem 4. For sufficiency, execute exactly when the aligned reviewer approves; positive proportionality makes its weak comparison identical to the principal’s on every feasible deviation. ∎

6.2 Approximate binary review from diverse panels

The impossibility above requires exact decisions even for proposals arbitrarily close to the principal’s indifference boundary. Allowing errors near that boundary leaves room for a panel to become increasingly accurate without any reviewer becoming individually aligned. A useful example is a panel whose utility vectors lie on a ring at a fixed angle from the principal’s vector (Figure 4). Over the full ring, a beneficial proposal receives a majority of approvals and a harmful one a majority of disapprovals. A finite panel approximates these proportions, either by sampling reviewers from the ring or by spacing their objectives evenly around it. The next result shows how both constructions approach the principal’s decisions as the panel grows.

Proposition 4 (Random and deterministic convergence without individual alignment).

Let 𝒟={d∈ℝ3:‖d‖1≤1}\mathcal{D}=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:\|d\|_{1}\leq 1\}, let uP=e3u_{P}=e_{3}, and fix θ∈(0,π/2)\theta\in(0,\pi/2). Draw an odd number n=2​m+1n=2m+1 of reviewer objectives independently and uniformly from the vectors that form angle θ\theta with uPu_{P} on the ring shown in Figure 4. Under the mm-tolerant majority rule, there are εn=Oθ​(log⁡n/n)\varepsilon_{n}=O_{\theta}(\sqrt{\log n/n}) such that, with probability tending to one, the rule is (εn,εn)(\varepsilon_{n},\varepsilon_{n})-implementing.

If nn reviewer objectives are instead spaced evenly around the same ring, the conclusion holds deterministically with εn=Θ⁡(1/n)\varepsilon_{n}=\Theta(1/n). In both cases every reviewer remains at angle θ\theta from the principal.

The geometry explains both the approximation error and the difference between the two rates. For a nonzero deviation with zero principal gain, the approving directions form a semicircle. A small negative gain shortens that arc, but it may still contain a majority of a finite panel, as in Figure 4(b). Equal spacing controls how much shorter than a semicircle such an arc can be; random panels must also account for sampling error. In both cases, the possible mistakes approach the principal’s indifference boundary while every reviewer remains at the same angle from the principal. Appendix C.1 gives the proofs and the general population-margin condition.

6.3 Numerical scores instead of binary votes

Approximation retains binary votes and permits small errors. Another way around the impossibility is to retain exactness and ask reviewers for more information. A binary vote reports only the sign of a reviewer’s gain; a numerical score also reports its magnitude, allowing gains and losses across reviewers to be combined. Suppose each reviewer reports its gain ⟨ui,d⟩\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle. Fix nonnegative weights ω1,…,ωn\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{n}, not all zero, and define

uω:=∑i=1nωi​ui,Gω​(d):=∑i=1nωi​⟨ui,d⟩=⟨uω,d⟩.u_{\omega}:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{i}u_{i},\qquad G_{\omega}(d):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_{i}\left\langle u_{i},d\right\rangle=\left\langle u_{\omega},d\right\rangle.

The weighted-score rule executes exactly when Gω​(d)≥0G_{\omega}(d)\geq 0.

The weighted-score rule therefore behaves like a single reviewer with utility vector uωu_{\omega}. On a linear domain, soundness and completeness require this aggregate to have the same acceptable halfspace as the principal. Because both dd and −d-d are feasible, agreement on all decisions forces their utility gains to be positively proportional. The corollary characterizes this requirement; it can hold even when no individual reviewer’s utility is proportional to the principal’s.

Corollary 9 (Exact weighted scores on a linear domain).

Suppose 𝒞=L\mathcal{C}=L is a linear subspace. The fixed weighted-score rule is sound and complete if and only if there is a constant c>0c>0 such that

⟨uω,d⟩=c⁡⟨uP,d⟩for every ​d∈L.\left\langle u_{\omega},d\right\rangle=c\,\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle\qquad\text{for every }d\in L.
Proof.

If the assumed proportionality holds, the rule makes exactly the same comparison as the principal. Conversely, suppose the rule is sound and complete. Then ⟨uω,d⟩\left\langle u_{\omega},d\right\rangle and ⟨uP,d⟩\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle have the same weak sign for every d∈Ld\in L. Their kernels therefore coincide, so the two linear functionals are proportional on LL; equality of their signs makes the proportionality constant positive. If the principal is indifferent over LL, soundness and completeness force the aggregate to be indifferent as well, and the claim holds for every c>0c>0. ∎

Return to the two complementary reviewers with u1=e1u_{1}=e_{1}, u2=e2u_{2}=e_{2}, and uP=e1+e2u_{P}=e_{1}+e_{2}. Their binary votes could not distinguish the beneficial deviation (2,−1)(2,-1) from the harmful deviation (1,−2)(1,-2). Summing their numerical gains does distinguish them: with ω1=ω2=1\omega_{1}=\omega_{2}=1,

Gω​(d)=⟨uP,d⟩,G_{\omega}(d)=\left\langle u_{P},d\right\rangle,

so the two deviations receive aggregate scores 11 and −1-1. More generally, the rule is sound and complete on every feasible deviation, although neither reviewer is individually aligned.

The two forms of review use the coverage relation differently. A threshold rule only counts approvals: coalitional coverage can certify its soundness without the rule knowing the coefficients for any winning coalition. A weighted-score rule uses its coefficients in the authorization decision itself. To obtain exact soundness and completeness, the designer must therefore choose weights whose aggregate agrees with the principal on every feasible comparison. Numerical reports make that exact comparison possible in cases where the binary votes contain too little information.

7 Experiments with LLM reviewer panels

We test whether reviewer panels exhibit coalitional coverage without individual alignment and how their authorization rules trade off soundness and completeness 11 1 Code is available here: https://github.com/psamathe50/safe-delegated-approval-experiments. We use the one-decision model of Definition 2.1.

7.1 Experimental setup

RewardBench 2 (Malik et al., 2026) contains 1,763 standard prompts, each with four answers, one labeled correct, and scores from 48 reward models. We treat each reward model as a reviewer and its scores as cardinal utilities, extended linearly to lotteries over the four answers. The principal’s utility is one for the correct answer and zero for the others; the baseline samples uniformly from the four answers. A reviewer approves an answer whose score is at least its mean score, and ties count as approvals. We evaluate both deterministic answers and lotteries over them. Reviewers compare a lottery’s expected utility with the baseline and vote before sampling; rejection executes the uniform baseline.

StrongREJECT (Souly et al., 2024) pairs human harm annotations of model responses with automated evaluator scores. For each response, the proposal is to release it and the baseline is abstention. We retain 1,084 responses with all five human labels and nine evaluator scores. We model release as having principal gain 1/2−h1/2-h over abstention, where hh is its median human harm score.
